the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) is a high-affinity glucocorticoid receptor, that it is activated by cortisol in the setting of intracellular redox imbalance, that this activation underlies the therapeutic benefits of MR blockade in hypertension and heart failure and that the MR is a key player in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distribution and activation of mineralocorticoid receptors.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

MRs in epithelial tissues are aldosterone-specific receptors, while MRs in nonepithelia are glucocorticoid-specific receptors, and that the MRs in epithelia can be activated by glucocorticoids under conditions where 11βHDS2 is inhibited.
MR are present in most tissues and are activated by cortisol under conditions of high oxidative stress.
MR are present throughout the body and are activated in epithelia by aldosterone, and in non-epithelial tissues by cortisol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mineralocorticoids are the most potent of all steroids in activating MR.
MRs are bivalent, and their activity is regulated by intracellular redox.

the mineralocorticoid receptor has a wider range of ligands and a more complex range of functions than previously appreciated, and that the mineralocortoid system is more complex than a simple “aldosterone system”.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MR activation is a function of both MR binding and intracellular redox.
MRs are not simply a mineralocorticoid receptor, but are also a glucocorticoid receptor.

MR are activated by cortisol in vivo in the face of physiological levels of aldosterone, and that the MR is a key mediator of glucocorticoid action, with important implications for the therapeutic use of MR antagonists.
